### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to evaluate LLMs' ability to identify missing information under underspecification by asking the minimally sufficient clarifying question. Papers [7], [8], [10], [12], [13], [20], and [24] all address clarifying question generation or ambiguity resolution in dialogue systems or question answering. However, these papers focus on resolving semantic ambiguity or generating clarifying questions for ambiguous queries, not underspecification specifically. Paper [9] introduces a benchmark for reasoning under missing or contradictory conditions, which overlaps conceptually with underspecification but does not focus on clarifying questions as the evaluation mechanism. None of the prior papers explicitly address the purpose of evaluating LLMs' ability to identify missing information under underspecification by asking the minimally sufficient clarifying question.

### Mechanism
The contribution formalizes underspecified reasoning tasks as constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs) with missing variable assignments, specifically as "1-sufficient CSPs" where acquiring exactly one variable's value determines the target. Papers [1], [2], [3], [5], [6], [11], [15], and [16] all discuss CSPs or extensions like valued CSPs, decomposition, or heuristic search. However, none of these papers define or use the specific concept of "1-sufficient CSPs" or apply CSPs to reasoning tasks framed as clarifying question selection. Paper [17] discusses constraint detection in natural language problem descriptions, which is tangentially related but does not formalize reasoning tasks as CSPs. Thus, the mechanism is not covered by prior work.

### Evaluation
The contribution provides a definitional/formal framework (known predicate, 1-sufficient CSP definitions) without quantitative metrics, enabling downstream benchmarks and difficulty metrics like search depth/width. Papers [14], [23], and [9] introduce benchmarks and evaluation metrics for CSPs or reasoning tasks, but none use the specific definitional framework proposed here. Papers [7], [8], [10], [12], [13], [20], and [24] evaluate clarifying question generation or ambiguity resolution using various metrics, but these are unrelated to the formal CSP framework. No prior paper uses the same evaluation design, so the evaluation is uncovered.

### Domain
The contribution operates in the domain of LLM reasoning, specifically underspecification and clarifying-question evaluation. Papers [7], [8], [10], [12], [13], [20], and [24] all address clarifying question generation or ambiguity resolution in dialogue systems or question answering, which falls within the same general application area. Paper [9] addresses reasoning under missing or contradictory conditions, which overlaps with underspecification. Therefore, the domain is covered.
